title: Cellular test for a natural categorical equivalence of simplicial-set functors
statement: Use simplicial sets, quasicategories and internal functor categories in a fixed universe as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A degreewise injective map is a simplicial map whose map in every simplicial degree is injective. Call a simplicial map $u:X\to Y$ a categorical equivalence if, for every quasicategory $\mathcal E$ in a sufficiently large universe, precomposition $\operatorname{Fun}(Y,\mathcal E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(X,\mathcal E)$ is an equivalence of quasicategories. Let $P,Q:\mathrm{sSet}\to\mathrm{sSet}$ be ordinary functors and $\eta:P\Rightarrow Q$ an ordinary natural transformation. Assume that both functors preserve degreewise injective maps and all small connected colimits: for every nonempty small indexing category whose underlying undirected graph is connected, the canonical maps from the colimits of $P$ and $Q$ applied to its diagrams to $P$ and $Q$ of their colimits are isomorphisms. If $\eta_{\varnothing}$ and $\eta_{\Delta^n}$ for every integer $n\geq0$ are categorical equivalences, then $\eta_K$ is a categorical equivalence for every small simplicial set $K$.

source.place: Agent-formulated general cellular criterion underlying the proof of Proposition 4.2.3; Corollary 1.3.10 and Corollaries 2.3.16, 2.3.18, 2.3.29 in the Joyal model structure. Read online, revision July 30, 2026. No Stacks tag states this quasicategorical result; WANTED: archived source.

proof.text: Work in the Joyal model structure of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. Every simplicial set is cofibrant, since its map from the empty simplicial set is degreewise injective. By [lem-coef-joyal-functor-equivalence-test], the categorical equivalences specified in the item are exactly the weak equivalences of this model structure. Call $L$ good when $\eta_L$ is such a weak equivalence. The hypotheses give goodness of the empty simplicial set and of every standard simplex. Goodness is invariant under a simplicial isomorphism $a:L\cong L\prime$: naturality expresses $\eta_{L\prime}=Q(a)\eta_LP(a)^{-1}$, and isomorphisms and composites of weak equivalences are weak equivalences.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.8; Definition 3.3.7 and Theorem 3.6.1; preparation for Proposition 4.2.3

proof.text:
Goodness is closed under a pushout $L=X\amalg_A B$ when $A\hookrightarrow B$ is degreewise injective and $X,A,B$ are good. The connected-colimit hypotheses identify the two image spans and their pushouts with $P(L)$ and $Q(L)$. Their specified legs are monomorphisms. Use the weak factorization systems in [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure] to prove the comparison directly. In the following finite construction all coproducts and pullbacks are constructed degreewise in simplicial sets; their compatible maps are given on representatives or tuples, so their universal properties hold. Trivial cofibrations are closed under pushout and composition: a lifting square from a pushout is the original square with the prescribed extra map, and two successive lifts solve a square for a composite. Trivial fibrations are closed under pullback and composition by pulling a lifting problem back and taking successive lifts. The two lifting-class characterizations in the cited node justify these closure assertions.

For a map $f:S\to T$ of spans $S=(X\leftarrow A\hookrightarrow B)$ and $T=(X'\leftarrow A'\hookrightarrow B')$ whose three components are weak equivalences, construct a span $R$ and maps $i:S\to R$, $s:T\to R$, $p:R\to T$ with $pi=f$ and $ps=1$. First factor $X\amalg X'\to X'$ (with components $f_X,1$) as a cofibration into $R_X$ followed by a trivial fibration $p_X:R_X\to X'$. Next factor $A\amalg A'\to A'\times_{X'}R_X$ as a cofibration into $R_A$ followed by a trivial fibration. The map on the $A$ summand is $(f_A,i_X\circ(A\to X))$ and that on the $A'$ summand is $(1,s_X\circ(A'\to X'))$. Projection defines $R_A\to R_X$ and $p_A:R_A\to A'$. The latter is a trivial fibration because the projection $A'\times_{X'}R_X\to A'$ is a pullback of $p_X$. Finally put $D=(B\amalg B')\amalg_{A\amalg A'}R_A$ and factor $D\to B'$ as a cofibration into $R_B$ followed by a trivial fibration $p_B$. The map from $R_A$ to $B'$ is $R_A\xrightarrow{p_A}A'\to B'$. This defines the span $R_X\leftarrow R_A\to R_B$ and the three span maps, with the claimed identities on each component. In particular $p$ is an objectwise weak equivalence, and two-out-of-three makes both $i$ and $s$ objectwise weak equivalences.

For $t=i$ or $t=s$, write its source span as $U=(U_X\leftarrow U_A\hookrightarrow U_B)$. Its maps $t_X,t_A$ are monomorphisms, since a coproduct injection followed by a cofibration is degreewise injective. The relative map $k_t:U_B\amalg_{U_A}R_A\to R_B$ is also monic: its map to $D$ is the pushout of the other source span's monomorphism $A'\hookrightarrow B'$ (for $t=i$) or $A\hookrightarrow B$ (for $t=s$), followed by the chosen cofibration $D\to R_B$. A pushout of an injective map is injective degreewise, because only boundary elements are identified with old elements and no two old elements are identified. As $t_A$ is a weak equivalence as well as a monomorphism, it is a trivial cofibration; hence $U_B\to U_B\amalg_{U_A}R_A$ is a trivial cofibration by the lifting argument above. Its composite with $k_t$ is $t_B$, a weak equivalence. Thus $k_t$ is a weak equivalence by two-out-of-three, and is therefore a trivial cofibration. Likewise $t_X$ is a trivial cofibration. The induced map on span pushouts factors as
$$U_X\amalg_{U_A}U_B\longrightarrow R_X\amalg_{U_A}U_B\cong R_X\amalg_{R_A}(R_A\amalg_{U_A}U_B)\longrightarrow R_X\amalg_{R_A}R_B.$$
The first arrow is a pushout of $t_X$ and the last a pushout of $k_t$, so both are trivial cofibrations. The middle isomorphism follows by giving the same three compatible maps out of either expression. Consequently the pushout maps induced by $i,s$ are weak equivalences. Since $ps=1$, two-out-of-three makes the pushout map induced by $p$ a weak equivalence too, and $pi=f$ proves that induced by $f$ is a weak equivalence. Apply this construction to the map of image spans given by $\eta_X,\eta_A,\eta_B$. Naturality identifies the resulting pushout comparison with the specified component $\eta_L$, since both agree on each pushout summand. This proves goodness of $L$.

source.place: Corollary 2.3.29; explicit finite factorization proof of its span comparison, using only the Joyal weak factorization systems. The argument is written out here instead of citing the cyclic generic comparison node.

proof.text: Goodness is closed under small nonzero limit-ordinal colimits. Let $\lambda$ be a small nonzero limit ordinal and $(L_\alpha)_{\alpha<\lambda}$ a diagram of good simplicial sets. Its ordinal category is nonempty and filtered: any two indices map to their maximum, and parallel arrows in a poset are equal. It is connected for the same reason. Thus $P,Q$ preserve its colimit, and the natural transformation $(\eta_{L_\alpha})$ is an objectwise Joyal weak equivalence by goodness. Apply [lem-coef-joyal-filtered-equivalences] to these two image diagrams. It gives a weak equivalence between their colimits; the preservation isomorphisms identify it with $\eta_{\operatorname{colim}L_\alpha}$, because both maps have the same composite with every structure map by naturality. This proves goodness of the colimit. In particular it applies to continuous chains of monomorphisms and to $\lambda=\omega$. A chain with no attachment has its starting object as endpoint; successor endpoints are handled by Step 2. The cited filtered-colimit theorem does not require monomorphism transitions, so no extra preservation hypothesis is imposed on $P,Q$.

source.place: Corollary 3.9.8, printed pp. 134-135: weak categorical equivalences are stable under all small filtered colimits.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-infinity-monomorphism-boundary-cells] to $\varnothing\hookrightarrow L$ to obtain subobjects $Z_0=\varnothing\hookrightarrow Z_1\hookrightarrow\cdots$ with colimit $L$, where stage $n$ attaches the nondegenerate $n$-simplices along their boundaries. The same statement applied to $\varnothing\hookrightarrow\partial\Delta^n$ constructs that boundary using cells of dimension less than $n$: a nondegenerate simplex of $\Delta^n$ corresponds to a strictly increasing vertex map, and one belongs to the boundary exactly when its image is a proper subset of $[n]$, so its dimension is less than $n$. For $n=0$ the boundary is empty. A stage attaching a small family $(\partial\Delta^n\to\Delta^n)_{t\in T}$ to $X$ can be refined to individual attachments: well-order $T$ with order type $\tau$ and put $V_\beta=X\amalg_{\coprod_{t<\beta}\partial\Delta^n}\coprod_{t<\beta}\Delta^n$ for $\beta\leq\tau$. Maps from $V_\beta$ to any simplicial set are exactly a map from $X$ and a map from each included cell agreeing on its boundary. This describes $V_0=X$, identifies each successor as a single-cell pushout and each nonzero limit as the colimit of its predecessors, and identifies $V_\tau$ with the original simultaneous attachment. These transition maps are monomorphisms: degreewise, each new cell glues in its complement of the boundary without identifying any old elements. This refinement is a construction in simplicial sets; no preservation of these coproducts by $P$ or $Q$ is asserted.

source.place: Theorem 1.3.8 and Corollary 1.3.10; explicit refinement of each boundary-cell stage by its universal property

proof.text: Prove by induction on $n\geq0$ that every simplicial set with no nondegenerate simplices of dimension greater than $n$ is good; the starting assertion in dimension $-1$ is the empty simplicial set. Assume the assertion in all lower dimensions. Step 4 constructs $\partial\Delta^n$ in finitely many stages of cells of dimensions less than $n$. Equivalently it has dimension at most $n-1$, so the inductive hypothesis makes it good (for $n=0$ use the empty-set hypothesis). Let $L$ have dimension at most $n$. In its filtration of Step 4, the stages before the $n$-cell attachment have dimension at most $n-1$, and hence are good; let $X=Z_n$ be the last of them. Refine the $n$-cell attachment to the continuous chain $(V_\beta)_{\beta\leq\tau}$ of Step 4. Induct on $\beta$: the base $V_0=X$ is good, a successor is good by Step 2 using goodness of $\partial\Delta^n$, $\Delta^n$ and $V_\beta$, and every nonzero limit is good by Step 3. The boundary inclusions into the standard simplices are monomorphisms, as are the transition maps by Step 4; the attaching maps from boundaries to the old base need not be monomorphisms. Thus $V_\tau=Z_{n+1}$ is good. All later stages add no cells and their maps are isomorphisms, since $L$ has no higher nondegenerate simplices; their colimit is $L$. Hence $L\cong Z_{n+1}$ is good. This proves the dimension induction, including arbitrary small infinite sets of cells in each fixed dimension.

source.place: Corollary 1.3.10, expanded dimension induction using Steps 2-4; the representable hypotheses remain the hypotheses of the item

proof.text: For arbitrary small $K$, use its boundary-cell sequence $(Z_n)$ from Step 4. Each $Z_n$ has dimension less than $n$: it is assembled from simplices of dimensions $0,\ldots,n-1$, and these simplices and their degeneracies contain no higher nondegenerate simplex. Thus Step 5 makes every $Z_n$ good, including $Z_0=\varnothing$. Its transitions are monomorphisms and its colimit is $K$. Step 3 for the nonzero limit ordinal $\omega$ gives that $\eta_K$ is a Joyal weak equivalence. By [lem-coef-joyal-functor-equivalence-test], precomposition by this very map is an equivalence of the entire functor quasicategories into every quasicategory in a sufficiently large universe. This is the conclusion with exactly the categorical-equivalence convention stated in the item.

source.place: Corollary 1.3.10 and Theorem 3.6.8; conclusion of the cellular reduction underlying Proposition 4.2.3
